newsitem.title: INDIA: India yet to bite the bullet on privatisation.
newsitem.headline: India yet to bite the bullet on privatisation.

text.p: India's centre-left coalition government is dragging its feet in implementing an ambitious programme to privatise state-run firms, the federal Disinvestment Commission and analysts said on Friday.

The privatisation panel also warned the government in a report that it would be hard pressed to muster a targeted 48 billion rupees ($1.34 billion) in disinvestment proceeds unless it swiftly pushed ahead with the programme.

"The Commission would like to point out that unless there is speedy implementation of the recommendations made...it would be difficult to achieve disinvestment of the order of 48 billion rupees as envisaged by the government for 1997/98 nor for the other objectives of the disinvestment process itself," it said.

India's partial privatisation programme suffered in 1996/97 (April-March) due to poor market conditions. The government expects to raise only five billion rupees in the year, against a target of 50 billion rupees.
Amir Ullah Khan, economist at a United Nations Development Programme project on Indian economic reforms, said the 15-party government's hands were tied when it came to privatisation.

"Can the government take any concrete measures without having severe pressure exerted upon it by the left?" he said, referring to two powerful Communist parties and other left-wing groups within the coalition who oppose rapid privatisation.

On Friday, trade unions from one firm listed for privatisation, Indian Telephone Industries Ltd, met Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and demanded he reject a proposal to sell off 74 percent of the company's shares to the public.

In another move that is certain to anger the coalition's left-wing partners, the Disinvestment Commission recommended the state-controlled telephone monopoly in Bombay and New Delhi, Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd, make a global depositary receipts issue of 10 percent of the state stake.
India began selling government stakes in state-controlled companies under an economic reform programme launched in 1991.

The government decided not to disinvest at all in firms involved in strategic areas such as atomic energy and space research, and sell up to 49 percent of firms in core sector areas like infrastructure.
In other areas, the government had decided to consider selling up to 74 percent of its stakes, losing its majority control.
The Disinvestment Commission said it was concerned that even when firms had been partially privatised, the government had failed to induct non-government officials into their boards of directors.

The panel also said it would defer a decision on privatising two state-controlled oil giants, Oil India Ltd (OIL) and the Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC), until the government decided to free domestic petroleum prices.
"The statement would definitely put a little pressure on the government to actually do it," R.K. Pachauri, director of the Tata Energy Research Institute, told Reuters.
India controls the domestic price of oil products, paying state-run firms a subsidy to sell their output at prices well below global prices.
Prime Minister Gujral said on Thursday that the oil subsidy bill, which mounted to 155 billion rupees in 1996/97, was unsustainable and an increase in petroleum prices was inevitable.

But the petroleum products price rise, suggested months ago, has also been stalled by strong resistance from the coalition government's left-wing partners, who say it will hurt the poor. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
